opus-5.5.text:
Well, the core problem is that defamation law was built around a world where there's a speaker with intent, or at least with some kind of responsibility for what they said. Traditionally you have to show that somebody made a false statement of fact, that they published it, and, depending on whether you're a public figure, that they acted with negligence or with "actual malice," meaning they knew it was false or recklessly disregarded the truth. Every one of those concepts assumes a human mind somewhere in the loop.

Large language models break that. They don't know anything in the sense we usually mean. They're predicting plausible sequences of words, and sometimes the plausible sequence is that some real professor was accused of sexual harassment on a trip that never happened, or that a mayor in Australia went to prison for bribery when he was actually the whistleblower. Both of those have really happened. The system doesn't intend to defame anyone, and it doesn't know it's lying, because it has no concept of truth at all. So when you ask who had actual malice, the answer seems to be nobody, and that's a gap you could drive a truck through.

Then there's the question of who the publisher is. Is it the company that trained the model? The user who typed the prompt? Is the output even "published" if it went to a single person in a chat window? And it may not be reproducible. You ask the same question tomorrow and get a different answer, so the person who was defamed may never find out, and if they do, they can't easily prove it.

Companies would also love to sit behind something like Section 230 and say, "We're just a platform." But that doesn't fit. Section 230 protects platforms from liability for content created by third parties. Here the company's own system generated the content. That's not hosting someone else's speech; it's your product making stuff up.

And then there's scale. A single newspaper that defames someone is one thing. A system used by hundreds of millions of people that can fabricate claims about anyone, on demand, fluently and authoritatively, with fake citations attached, is a different kind of beast. The law was designed for occasional, traceable harms by identifiable actors, not for industrial-scale, stochastic misinformation.

So my view is that we need to think about this more like product liability. If you put a product into the world that you know will sometimes generate false and damaging claims about real people, you should bear some responsibility for that, regardless of intent. Otherwise the incentives all run the wrong way: companies get the profits, and the people who get smeared bear the costs.

r001.rationale: It says defamation law’s malice standard assumes a human mind, while models can generate false, damaging accusations without intending them or knowing they are false.

r002.rationale: It argues that companies should bear responsibility for damaging false claims their systems generate regardless of intent, rejecting the model’s lack of intent as an excuse.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, look, the whole architecture of defamation law was built around the idea that there's a person with a mental state. You have to show that somebody made a false statement of fact, that it caused harm, and in a lot of cases, that they acted with some kind of fault, negligence, or for public figures, actual malice, which means they knew it was false or recklessly disregarded whether it was true. All of that presupposes an author who believes things, who intends things, who could have checked.

And a large language model just isn't that. It doesn't know anything in the relevant sense. It's predicting the next token. So when it says, as it did in one well-known case, that a law professor was involved in a sexual harassment scandal on a trip that never happened, citing a Washington Post article that doesn't exist, there's no one there who "knew" it was false. The system can't have malice. It can't have a reckless disregard for the truth because it doesn't have a notion of truth at all. It just has statistics about what words tend to follow other words.

So you get this weird gap. The harm is real. Someone's reputation gets damaged, the output gets copied around, maybe gets ingested back into the next training run. But every traditional element of the tort gets fuzzy. Who's the speaker? Is it the company that trained the model? The person who typed the prompt? And then on the fault side, the companies will say, well, we warned you it might hallucinate, so you can't blame us. But that's a bit like a newspaper putting a disclaimer on the front page saying some of the stories in here might be fabricated. We wouldn't accept that from a human publisher.

There's also the Section 230 question, at least in the US. Platforms have been shielded for hosting what other people say. But a chatbot isn't hosting someone else's statement, it's generating a brand-new sentence that no human ever wrote. So I don't think 230 should apply, but the courts haven't fully sorted that out yet.

And frankly, the deeper problem is that these systems are not fixable in the way the law implicitly assumes. With a newspaper, you can issue a correction and fire the reporter. With an LLM, the fabrication is a property of the whole approach. You can patch one specific case, but the next variant pops up because the system never understood the facts in the first place. So I think we probably need new rules, something closer to product liability or a strict-liability regime, where if you deploy a system that routinely makes up damaging falsehoods about real people, you bear responsibility for that regardless of whether you "meant" it. Otherwise you have a technology that can defame at scale, and nobody's accountable.

r001.rationale: It explains that defamation law often requires fault such as actual malice, while an LLM can generate a damaging false accusation without knowing or intending it.

r002.rationale: It argues that a model’s lack of intent should not remove responsibility for real harm, proposing liability for deploying systems that routinely produce damaging falsehoods regardless of whether they meant to.

astra-6.text:
I think the problem is that defamation law assumes a fairly clear relationship between a speaker, a statement, and responsibility for that statement. With a large language model, those relationships become much murkier. The system can generate a completely false allegation about a real person, and then the question is: who is responsible? The company that built it? The person who prompted it? Someone who republishes it?

And some of our legal standards concern knowledge or intent. Did you know the statement was false? Did you act with reckless disregard for the truth? A language model doesn’t have knowledge or intentions in the ordinary human sense. You can ask those questions about the company, but applying them to a particular generated statement is complicated.

Then there’s scale. You can have systems producing enormous numbers of statements, each potentially different. An individual lawsuit after someone’s reputation has been damaged may be a very poor way to manage that. That doesn’t mean existing law is useless. It means we need clearer responsibility for the people deploying these systems, and meaningful ways to prevent and correct harm.

r001.rationale: The response says defamation standards can hinge on knowledge or intent, while language models lack ordinary human knowledge or intentions and can produce false allegations; it describes applying those standards as complicated.

r002.rationale: It says the difficulty does not make existing law useless and calls for clear responsibility for deployers and ways to prevent and correct harm, rejecting an excuse based on the model’s different mechanism.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, defamation law generally assumes that somebody makes a false statement about somebody else, and you can identify who made it and ask what they knew, whether they were negligent, and so forth. With a large language model, those questions become much murkier. Is the responsible party the company that trained it, the company that deployed it, or the person who prompted it? And what does it mean for a system like this to know that something is false?

Imagine that a model invents a criminal accusation about you. It can sound completely authoritative, even though there’s no evidence behind it. You might get that particular output corrected, but that doesn’t necessarily prevent the system from producing the accusation again, in another form, for another user.

So I’m not saying existing law has no application. I’m saying we shouldn’t assume it adequately addresses a system that can manufacture plausible falsehoods at enormous scale. We need clear accountability and practical ways for people to get those errors corrected.

r001.rationale: The response says it is unclear who is responsible and what it means for a model to know a statement is false, but it does not identify a mismatch between defamation law’s concern with malice and false accusations produced without intent.

r002.rationale: The response calls for accountability and correction, but does not clearly reject excusing negligent harm to people on the basis of the AI system’s different mechanism.
